lesson.menu_title: The Culture Question — Fit, Values and How You Lead
lesson.menu_desc: Answering the people questions with the same precision as the numbers, and saying what you prefer without sounding rigid -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- The Culture Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 17 -- The Culture Question
lesson.grammar_point: would rather, had better and may as well

listenings.text: When I ask a finance candidate about culture, I am not looking for the right adjectives. Everybody is collaborative and everybody has an open door. What I listen for is one real moment. A time somebody on his team disagreed with him, and what he did the next morning. The strong candidates give me that moment in under a minute, and they tell it with the other person in the story, not only themselves. The weak ones give me a list of values. And the ones I remember are the ones who say what they would rather do, and why, without pretending there is only one way to lead.

I spent fourteen years as a finance director before I started coaching, and the culture question was the one I prepared least. That was a mistake. In a final round, the numbers have already been checked. What is left is whether people want to work with you on a bad Tuesday. My advice now is simple. Pick one habit that shows how you lead, and tell it with a name and a date. If you have changed, say so. I used to check every line myself, and these days I would rather give my team the problem than the answer. That sentence does more in a culture interview than any list of values.

extra_audio.text: Laura asks how his last team would describe him. He gives two adjectives and offers two names to call. She asks whether finance leaders micromanage, and he says what he used to do and what he does now. She says decisions take time there. He suggests they agree early on which decisions are his.
